1.q: בְּ⁠רֵאשִׁ֗ית מַמְלְכ֛וּת יְהוֹיָקִ֥ים בֶּן־יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה
1.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reign**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the time of ruling by]

Jeremiah is using the word translated as **this word was** to continue introducing the new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4.

Jeremiah is using the word **saying** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. This also occurs in verses 11, 12, and 17.

2.note: See how you translated **Thus says Yahweh** in 2:5. This also occurs in verses 4 and 18.

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, command you, Jeremiah, to stand in the courtyard of my house]

Here, **all the cities of Judah** represents all the people who live in the cities of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to all the people from the cities of Judah]
Here, the word **to** marks **to bow down** as the goal or purpose of the people of Judah who are **coming**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:26. This also occurs in verses 7, 9, and 10.
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:14.

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **take away**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Speak every word that I have commanded you]

3.note: Although the term **a man** is masculine, Yahweh is using the word in a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:22.
See how you translated this expression in 4:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:12.

4.note: The pronoun **you** refers to Jeremiah while the pronoun **them** refers to the Judeans. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And you, Jeremiah, shall say to the people of Judah]

4.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה אִם־לֹ֤א תִשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֵלַ֔⁠י
4.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall tell them that Yahweh says, “If you do not listen to me]

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that the people of Judah will not listen to him and will not walk in his law. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If it happens that you do not listen to me]

Yahweh is using **to walk in my law** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to obey my law.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to obey my law]
Here, **to the face of you** represents before you. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before you]

5.note: Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the prophets whom he sent persistently and the refusal of the people to listen. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [yet you have not listened]
See how you translated **rising early and sending** in 25:4.

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as Yahweh allowed his sanctuary at **Shiloh** to be destroyed, so he will allow **this house** to be destroyed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [then I will allow this house to be destroyed, just as I allowed my sanctuary at Shiloh to be destroyed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **curse**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as something accursed]

Yahweh is saying **for all the nations of the earth** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [for the people of many nations on the earth]

7.q: וַֽ⁠יִּשְׁמְע֛וּ הַ⁠כֹּהֲנִ֥ים וְ⁠הַ⁠נְּבִאִ֖ים וְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֑ם אֶֽת־יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ מְדַבֵּ֛ר אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֥ים הָ⁠אֵ֖לֶּה בְּ⁠בֵ֥ית יְהוָֽה
7.note: The words that the ULT translates as **And** indicates that the priests, the prophets, and all the people **heard** Jeremiah at the same time as he **was speaking these words** in the house of Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah while he was speaking these words in the house of Yahweh]

Jeremiah is using the term **words** to represent what he said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this prophet say what Yahweh commanded him to say to them]

8.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The priests, the prophets, and the people are repeating forms of the verb **die** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You will surely die]

9.note: The priests, the prophets, and the people are using the question form to accuse Jeremiah of speaking wrongly. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have prophesied in the name of Yahweh, saying, ‘Like Shiloh this house will be, and this city will be desolate without a dweller’!]
See how you translated this phrase in 3:17. This also occurs in verses 16 and 20.

The point of this comparison is that just as the sanctuary at **Shiloh** was destroyed, so **this house** will be destroyed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [This house will be destroyed just as the sanctuary at Shiloh was destroyed]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that this house will be like Shiloh]

The phrases **desolate** and **without a dweller** express a single idea. The expression **without a dweller** tells more about **desolate**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [this city will be totally desolate, with no one living in it]

10.note: Here Jeremiah is introducing **the officials of Judah** as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [some men who were official leaders of Judah]

The implication is that the officials sat down at the entrance of the gate in order to judge Jeremiah’s case. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they sat down to judge the case in the entrance of the New Gate of Yahweh]

11.q: מִשְׁפַּט־מָ֨וֶת֙ לָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה כִּ֤י נִבָּא֙ אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר שְׁמַעְתֶּ֖ם בְּ⁠אָזְנֵי⁠כֶֽם
11.note: The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This man has prophesied against this city, just as you have heard with your ears. Therefore, a judgment of death to this man]

The priests and the prophets are using **A judgment of death** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a sentence of death.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A death sentence]

Here, **with your ears** represents hearing something personally. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verse 15. Alternate translation: [for yourselves]

13.note: See how you translated this expression in 7:3.

Here, **the voice of Yahweh** represents what Yahweh says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and obey the words of Yahweh]

Jeremiah is not using this possessive form **your God** to indicate that the people of Judah possess or control Yahweh. Rather Jeremiah is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the people of Judah worship. This also occurs in verse 16. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom you worship]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disaster**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verses 3 and 19. Alternate translation: [concerning the disastrous things]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:23.

14.note: Here, **your hand** represents the power and control that the officials and the people have over Jeremiah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at your mercy]

Jeremiah is using **behold me in your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am in your power.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am at your mercy] or [you have power over me]

Jeremiah is using the adjectives **the good** and **the right** as nouns to mean certain kinds of actions. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [according to what seems good and according to what seems right]

Jeremiah is using **in your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in your judgment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your judgment]

15.note: Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **know** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you must certainly know]

15.q: אִם־מְמִתִ֣ים אַתֶּם֮ אֹתִ⁠י֒ כִּי־דָ֣ם נָקִ֗י אַתֶּם֙ נֹתְנִ֣ים עֲלֵי⁠כֶ֔ם
15.note: Jeremiah is presenting a possible condition, that the officials and the people will put him to death. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [if you put me to death, you will bring the guilt of innocent blood upon yourselves]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [truly]

16.q: וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֤וּ הַ⁠שָּׂרִים֙ וְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֔ם אֶל־הַ⁠כֹּהֲנִ֖ים וְ⁠אֶל־הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֑ים אֵין־לָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ מִשְׁפַּט־מָ֔וֶת כִּ֗י בְּ⁠שֵׁ֛ם יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ דִּבֶּ֥ר אֵלֵֽי⁠נוּ
16.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And the officials and all the people said to the priests and to the prophets, “Because he has spoken to us in the name of Yahweh our God, there is no judgment of death for this man.”]

Here, **the name of Yahweh our God** represents the authority of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by the authority of Yahweh our God]

17.note: Here Jeremiah is introducing **men from the elders of the land** as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [there were some elders of the land who]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **elders** that are characterized by belonging to **the land**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from among the elders who lived in the land]

18.q: מיכיה הַ⁠מּ֣וֹרַשְׁתִּ֔י הָיָ֣ה נִבָּ֔א בִּ⁠ימֵ֖י חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה
18.note: Here the elders are providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
The word **Micah** is the name of a man, and the word **Morashtite** describes him as a person from the town of Moresheth.

18.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת צִיּ֞וֹן שָׂדֶ֤ה תֵֽחָרֵשׁ֙
18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies said that Zion will be plowed like a field]
See how you translated this phrase in 25:8.

18.q: צִיּ֞וֹן שָׂדֶ֤ה תֵֽחָרֵשׁ֙ וִ⁠ירוּשָׁלַ֨יִם֙ עִיִּ֣ים תִּֽהְיֶ֔ה וְ⁠הַ֥ר הַ⁠בַּ֖יִת לְ⁠בָמ֥וֹת יָֽעַר
18.note: These three clauses mean basically the same thing. The second and the third emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Zion and Jerusalem and the mountain of the house will all be left in ruins]

Yahweh is speaking of Zion as if it were **a field** that enemies would plow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, or you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternate translation: [Enemies will destroy Zion like farmers plow up a field]

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the mountain of the house will become high places of a forest]

19.note: The elders are using the question form to remind the people that Hezekiah and the people of Judah did not put Micah to death. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah, king of Judah, and all Judah did not put him to death at all!]

The elders are repeating forms of the verb translated as **Putting to death** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah actually put him to death]

19.q: הֲ⁠לֹא֮ יָרֵ֣א אֶת־יְהוָה֒ וַ⁠יְחַל֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה
19.note: The elders are using the question form to emphasize that Hezekiah did fear Yahweh and seek his favor. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [He certainly feared Yahweh and entreated the face of Yahweh]

19.q: הֲ⁠לֹא֮ יָרֵ֣א אֶת־יְהוָה֒ וַ⁠יְחַל֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה
19.note: This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **fear**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [He feared Yahweh and entreated the face of Yahweh]

The elders are using **entreat the face of Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “beg Yahweh to be merciful.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [beg Yahweh to be merciful]
The pronoun **we** refers to the elders and the other people of Judah who are speaking. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But we people of Judah are doing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [very wicked deeds]

20.note: Here Jeremiah is introducing **Uriah, son of Shemaiah** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [A man named Uriah, the son of Shemaiah, who was from the town of Kiriath Jearim]
The words **Uriah** and **Shemaiah** are the names of men, and **Kiriath Jearim** is the name of a town.

22.note: The words **Elnathan** and **Akbor** are the names of men.

23.note: The pronoun **he** refers to King Jehoiakim, and the pronoun **him** refers to Uriah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Jehoiakim struck Uriah with the sword and threw Uriah’s corpse]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:21.

Jeremiah is using **the graves of the sons of the people** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the burial place for ordinary people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the burial place for ordinary people]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:19.

24.q: אַ֗ךְ יַ֚ד אֲחִיקָ֣ם בֶּן־שָׁפָ֔ן הָיְתָ֖ה אֶֽת־יִרְמְיָ֑הוּ לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֛י תֵּת־אֹת֥⁠וֹ בְ⁠יַד־הָ⁠עָ֖ם לַ⁠הֲמִיתֽ⁠וֹ
24.note: Jeremiah uses the word **However** here to indicate a contrast between what happened to Uriah and what happened to Jeremiah. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [In contrast to this, the hand of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, was with Jeremiah]

Here, **the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan** represents the protection and support that Ahikam gave to Jeremiah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Ahikam, son of Shaphan, protected Jeremiah]

The statement **the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah** is a comment about what happened after the story as a result of the events within the story itself. This signals the end of a story. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of a story. Alternate translation: [in the end, Ahikam, son of Shaphan, supported and protected Jeremiah]

Here, **the hand of the people** represents the power and control of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the control of the people]
